title: It's too expensive
setting: A salesperson meets a price objection on the fourth call.

lines.t: We like the programme, but honestly, it's too expensive.
Too expensive compared to what?
Compared to doing nothing, I suppose. We tried training two years ago.
And what happened?
People stopped attending after three weeks. We paid for the whole thing.
So the real question isn't price. It's whether it will happen this time.
That's fair.
Then let's start with one department, and tie the rest to attendance.
Meaning if attendance drops, we stop?
No penalty. If it works, we continue. Would that be easier to approve?
Considerably. Send it that way and I'll walk it through myself.

title: Qualifying the lead
setting: A first call with a company that downloaded a guide.

lines.t: Thanks for making time. You downloaded our assessment guide last week.
Yes, I was curious. We have people who struggle on calls in English.
How many people, roughly?
Maybe twenty in customer service.
And is there a budget for training this year?
There's a training budget, but I don't control it.
Who does?
The operations director. She signs off anything over five thousand.
Would it help if I prepared a short summary you could forward to her?
That would help a lot. One page, if possible.
One page it is. I'll send it today and follow up on Thursday.

title: The person who answers
setting: A sales manager goes through yesterday's calls with a rep.

lines.t: How many did you call yesterday?
Thirty. Four conversations.
That's a cold call list. Where do the warm leads come from?
The webinar. Eleven prospects gave us a real email address.
Then warm up a lead properly before you ring. Read what they downloaded.
The problem is the gatekeeper. I never get past her.
She isn't the obstacle you think. Ask her who owns the decision and she'll usually tell you.
And if the decision maker isn't the budget holder?
Then you have two conversations. That's what prospecting looks like in any company over fifty people.
So I qualify a lead first, and the demo comes after that.

title: Twelve deals, four real
setting: Monday morning, and the numbers on the screen do not match reality.

lines.t: Your sales pipeline says twelve deals. How many are real?
Four.
Then fix the CRM today. A pipeline review built on fiction wastes everybody's Monday.
Some of them I just haven't touched in a while.
How long is our sales cycle?
Nine weeks, roughly.
And the last touchpoint on the ones you called real?
Two of them, June.
Then they're gone. Move them out and book a discovery call with the ones still breathing.
I'll make the follow-up calls this afternoon, and the demo for Burgas is Thursday.

title: Forty seconds in a lift
setting: A rep has fifteen minutes with a client and twenty slides.

lines.t: They gave me fifteen minutes on Thursday.
Then your pitch is eight minutes and the rest belongs to them.
I have twenty slides.
You have four. What's your elevator pitch?
We help mid-size firms cut invoice processing from six days to one.
That's good. Say it in the first forty seconds, then stop talking.
And if they look unconvinced?
Walk the client through one real example, slowly. A soft sell with a real number beats a hard sell with twenty slides.
Nobody enjoys the hard sell anyway.
People don't mind being sold to. They mind being talked at for fifteen minutes.

title: Too expensive
setting: A rep reports that the objection is price, as always.

lines.t: Their objection is price. It's always price.
Is it? Or is that the polite version?
He said 'it's too expensive' and went quiet.
That's usually a stall. Ask him what he's comparing it to.
And if he pushes back again?
Then you handle the objection with a question. A discount is the last thing you reach for, if ever.
What question?
'If the price were right, would you be starting in March?' His answer tells you whether price is the real issue.
And if he says no?
Then price was never the deal breaker, and you've saved yourself three weeks of chasing.

title: The pen was already out
setting: A client asked about timing and the rep sent an email instead.

lines.t: How did Burgas end?
She asked how quickly we could start.
That's a buying signal, and you walked past it.
I sent a summary email instead.
When somebody asks about timing, try a trial close. 'If we start on the 3rd, does that work for your team?'
It felt pushy.
It's a question, and she raised the date herself.
So how do I close the sale without inventing urgency?
Use the urgency she already has. Her system stops being supported in May, and she told you that in the first meeting.
Then I'll ask her to sign on the dotted line this month, and we cross the line on a deal that started in February.

title: The one we lost in May
setting: A quarterly review of one rep's numbers.

lines.t: You hit target in three of the last four quarters.
The fourth one still annoys me.
Your win rate is 31%, which is above the team.
And my deal size is below it.
That's the honest problem. More small deals, more work, same commission.
So I should chase bigger companies.
Chase companies with a budget holder in the room. Size follows.
What about the lost deal in May? I still don't know why.
Call him and ask. People tell you the truth once there's nothing left to sell them.
And if we lost on price, I'll stop discounting to reach quota next time.

title: Three hundred kilometres
setting: A rep's area has grown and one client has gone quiet.

lines.t: My territory now runs from Ruse to Burgas.
Three hundred kilometres and eleven clients.
Two of them are key accounts. The rest I see twice a year.
How many renewals fall before March?
Four. Three will sign, one has gone quiet.
Quiet before a renewal usually means somebody else has called them.
Should I drive out and see him?
Go this week. Keeping him costs less than trying to win back a customer in June.
And if he's already decided?
Then you'll know why, and so will the next account manager who takes that client.

title: Eleven pages
setting: A formal tender arrives with forty questions attached.

lines.t: Their request for proposal is forty questions long.
How much of it matters?
Six questions. The rest is procurement protecting itself.
Answer all forty, and put the six on the first page.
My proposal runs to eleven pages.
Make the scope of work exact. Most arguments in month three begin in a vague sentence in month one.
They'll ask for a discount.
They always do. Hold the price and change what's included.
Isn't that the same thing?
Value-based pricing sets the number by what it's worth to them. A no-brainer offer is one where they can see that for themselves.
